638.title: I have overcome the world (John 16:16–33)
638.hook: sorrow turns to joy like a woman after labor
638.howItsDone: Christians often turn to John 16:33 in hard seasons, as a word of courage spoken before the worst had happened.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Advocate, the one called to your side. Your line was into all truth. Did you take one step on that decision? Day six hundred thirty-eight.

"A little while." Jesus says it, and the disciples start whispering to each other across the table. What does he mean, a little while? A little while and you won't see me, and again a little while and you will. They want to ask him, but nobody does. It's late, he's been talking about leaving all evening, and every new sentence seems to make things more confusing. But he notices them whispering. He knows what they want to ask. And instead of a definition, he gives them a picture. One that anyone who has been in a delivery room will recognize.
screen: `A LITTLE WHILE? WHAT DOES HE MEAN?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world." Travail is labor. And notice what the picture does. The pain isn't swapped out for something else. The same event that hurts is the event that brings the joy. The sorrow turns into joy, the way labor turns into a baby in your arms. The prophets used this image too, for Israel waiting on God's new day. Jesus applies it to the next few days. They will weep while others rejoice. Then they'll see him again, "and your joy no man taketh from you." Then the chapter's last line, the one in today's carry: "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world." Two honest halves. You will have trouble: no promise that life gets easy. And then, be of good cheer. The Greek is tharseite: take courage, be brave, cheer up. It's the same word he says elsewhere in the Gospels to frightened people. And the reason: I have overcome. The Greek verb is nikao, to win, to conquer. You may know the related word nike, victory. And it's in a tense that speaks of something already done. He says it the night before the cross, before anything looks like winning. Christians hear in that the heart of their hope: the victory is spoken before it is seen.
screen: `THE SAME EVENT THAT HURTS BRINGS JOY.`
`NIKAO: SPOKEN BEFORE IT LOOKS LIKE WINNING.`
then, large: `BE OF GOOD CHEER; I HAVE OVERCOME THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take heart in one trouble. Settle, and breathe. Name one trouble you're in right now. Not the whole list. One. Say it plainly to yourself, the way Jesus says it: in the world you will have this. Don't pretend it's smaller than it is. Then breathe in, and on the out-breath, let yourself hear the second half: take courage. Do it a few times. If you pray, you can bring that trouble to God with his words: be of good cheer. If you don't, simply let courage sit beside the trouble. The bell holds the time.
Nikao. The Greek verb behind I have overcome: to win, to conquer, related to the word for victory, nike.
Your line: be of good cheer. Today, when the trouble you named shows up, say both halves to yourself: this is real, and take courage. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

639.title: The hour has come (John 17:1–5)
639.hook: he lifts his eyes and prays for the Father's glory
639.howItsDone: Many churches read John 17 in the days between Ascension and Pentecost, and some Christians pray standing with eyes and hands lifted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman in labor, and words spoken before the victory showed: nikao, I have overcome. Your line was be of good cheer. How did your trouble look with courage beside it? Day six hundred thirty-nine.

For three chapters Jesus has been talking to his friends. Now, suddenly, he stops talking to them and starts talking to God, out loud, while they listen. The prayer fills the whole of John seventeen. Christians often call it the High Priestly Prayer, because in it he stands between God and his friends, the way a priest does. And it starts with a small physical detail John doesn't want you to miss. He looks up.

In the King James Bible: "These words spake Jesus, and lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee." John has shown this before: at Lazarus's tomb, too, Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, Father. And then the first words: the hour is come. If you've been reading John from the start, that line lands hard. At the wedding at Cana, Jesus told his mother, mine hour is not yet come. More than once, people tried to seize him, and they couldn't, John says, because his hour had not yet come. Then, a few chapters back, when some Greeks came looking for him, he said it at last: the hour is come. The whole Gospel has been counting down to this. And what is the hour for? Glory. In John, that word does something unexpected. The glory isn't a throne or a crown. In John's telling it is bound up with the cross: the moment that looks like shame is the moment John calls glory. Then comes a definition, and it's the line in today's carry: "And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent." Notice it doesn't define eternal life as living forever, or as a place you go after you die. It defines it as knowing. And knowing, in the Bible, is often close and personal: the way you know a friend, not a fact. So for John, eternal life can begin now, in a relationship, not only later.
screen: `HE LIFTS HIS EYES, AS AT LAZARUS'S TOMB.`
`NOT YET, NOT YET, AND NOW THE HOUR.`
`IN JOHN, THE GLORY IS THE CROSS.`
then, large: `FATHER, THE HOUR IS COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lift your eyes as you pray. If you can, stand up, or sit straight, and slowly lift your face. Look at the ceiling, or out a window at the sky. Notice how different it feels from looking down at a screen, or at the floor. Breathe there. If you pray, you can pray with your eyes lifted the way he did, even just the word Father. If you don't, simply let your eyes rest on something high and wide, and let your thoughts get bigger than the day so far. The bell holds the time.
Hora. John's word for the hour, the moment the whole Gospel has been counting toward: the cross, which John calls glory.
Your line: this is life eternal. Today, spend ten unhurried minutes really getting to know someone, and notice that knowing is a kind of life. Day six hundred thirty-nine.

640.title: Keep them (John 17:6–19)
640.hook: he prays for his friends: not out of the world, but kept from evil
640.carry: in the world, but not of it
640.tomorrow: that they may all be one
640.howItsDone: Many Christians pray for friends and family by name every day, some with a written list, and intercession, praying for others, is part of almost every Christian service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he lifted his eyes and said, hora, the hour is come. Your line was this is life eternal: knowing, not just lasting. Who did you get to know a little better? Day six hundred forty.

If you've ever overheard someone praying for you, you know it's a strange and tender thing. A grandmother at the kitchen table who didn't know you'd come in. A parent at the hospital door. A friend who says, I've been praying for you, and means it. You're hearing what they say about you when they're talking to God, not to you. That's what the disciples get at this table. Jesus prays for them out loud, while they're sitting right there. And what he asks for them is not what you might expect.
screen: `THE DISCIPLES HEAR IT AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: He begins by describing them, and it's generous. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. These are the same friends who argued about who was greatest, who didn't understand half of what he said, and one of whom will deny him tonight. He talks about them as faithful anyway. Then the center of the prayer: "Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are." Keep. The Greek word is tereo: to watch over, to guard, to keep safe, the word for a guard keeping watch. And he says that while he was with them, he kept them himself. Now he's leaving, so he hands the job to the Father. Then the line that surprises people: "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil." He could have asked for an escape. Get them out of here, somewhere safe. He doesn't. He wants them to stay in the middle of things, and be guarded there. Some translations say from the evil one; the Greek can be read either way, as evil or as the evil one, and scholars differ. Then: "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth." Sanctify means to set apart, make holy. And a few lines later he says, as you sent me into the world, so I've sent them into the world. Not out of the world. Into it. Christians often sum this up with a phrase drawn from these verses: in the world, but not of it.
screen: `NOT OUT OF THE WORLD, BUT KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your friends by name. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind three friends, one at a time. Picture each face. Think about where each of them is today: the job, the worry, the place they can't escape. Don't wish them out of it. Wish them kept in it. If you pray, you can say his words over each one, by name: keep them. If you don't, hold each friend in mind for a few breaths and wish them safe where they are. The bell holds the time.
Keep them. Jesus asks the Father to guard his friends, not by taking them out of the world, but by keeping them safe in it.
Your line: in the world, but not of it. Today, send one of those three friends a message: I was thinking of you today. Day six hundred forty.

screen: `DAY 640 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THAT THEY MAY ALL BE ONE.`

641.title: That they may all be one (John 17:20–26)
641.hook: he prays for all who will believe, that they may be one
641.howItsDone: Churches in many places keep a yearly Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, often in January, when Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians pray together, often using the words of John 17:21.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he prayed for his friends to be guarded, not removed. Your line was in the world, but not of it. Did you send that message? Day six hundred forty-one.
screen: `IN THE WORLD, BUT NOT OF IT.`

segments.voice: Up to now, Jesus has been praying for the people at the table. Eleven men, tired and confused, a few hours before the worst night of their lives. Then the prayer widens. He looks past the room, past that night, past the century, and prays for people who haven't been born yet. Christians hear themselves in this line. If you've ever been in a church, or a choir, or a Bible study, or anywhere people pray in his name, this is the moment Christians say he prayed for you.

In the King James Bible: "Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word; That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." Look at the shape of that. The model for oneness is not an organization. It's the bond between the Father and the Son: you in me, and I in you. And the purpose is outward: that the world may believe. The way Christians treat each other is meant to say something to everyone watching. Here's the honest part. Christians have not always lived this prayer. Churches of the East and West parted ways. The Reformation brought more divisions. Today there are a great many separate church bodies, and Christians in many of them name that as a real grief. This verse has also been a seed. In more recent times, churches that had long been apart began talking, praying together, and in some cases reuniting. That movement is often called ecumenism. When Pope John Paul the Second wrote a letter on Christian unity in 1995, he titled it with this verse in Latin: Ut unum sint, that they may be one. Protestant and Orthodox voices for unity quote it too. Churches still differ, honestly, on what that unity should look like: one visible church, or many churches recognizing each other, or a shared life in the Spirit across different names. The prayer itself doesn't spell it out.
screen: `ONE, AS THE FATHER AND SON ARE ONE.`
`UT UNUM SINT: A SEED FOR UNITY.`
then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Christian unity. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a church that isn't yours, or isn't the kind you know best. A cathedral, a storefront chapel, an Orthodox church with icons, a house church, a church in another country. Picture the people there this week: singing, arguing about the budget, bringing casseroles. If you pray, you can say his words for them and for your own: that they all may be one. If you don't, simply hold them in goodwill for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Ecumenism. The modern movement toward Christian unity that this prayer, that they may all be one, became a seed for.
Your line: that they may be one. Today, say one generous thing about a Christian tradition that isn't the one you know best. Day six hundred forty-one.

642.title: Whom do you seek? (John 18:1–11)
642.hook: soldiers with torches; he steps forward: I am he, and they fall back
642.howItsDone: Many churches read John's account of the arrest during Holy Week, and on Good Friday in a number of traditions the whole Passion according to John is read or sung aloud, often with different readers taking the parts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer widened to everyone who would ever believe, the seed of what's now called ecumenism. Your line was that they may be one. What generous thing did you say? Day six hundred forty-two.

The prayer is over. They walk out into the dark, across the brook Kidron, into a garden on the other side. John says Judas knew the place, because Jesus often went there with his friends. And Judas comes. With him, a band of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, carrying lanterns and torches and weapons. A quiet garden at night, and suddenly a line of firelight moving through it. And Jesus doesn't wait to be found.

John tells it this way, in the King James Bible: Jesus, "knowing all things that should come upon him, went forth, and said unto them, Whom seek ye?" He steps forward. They answer, Jesus of Nazareth. And he says two words: I am he. Then something strange happens. "As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground." Why would armed men fall over? Look at the Greek. What he says is ego eimi, I am. The he is added in English to make the sentence smooth; many printings of the King James put it in italics to show it isn't in the Greek. And all through John's Gospel, I am has been doing heavy lifting. I am the bread of life. I am the light of the world. Before Abraham was, I am. Some readers hear in it an echo of God's name given to Moses at the burning bush, I AM. So when the soldiers stagger back, John seems to be showing who is really in charge in this garden. Not the soldiers. Then Jesus asks again, and this time he bargains, not for himself, but for his friends: if you're looking for me, let these go their way. Peter has other ideas. He pulls a sword and cuts off the right ear of the high priest's servant. Only John gives us the servant's name: Malchus. And Jesus says: "Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?" No fighting. He walks into it with his eyes open.
screen: `I AM HE, AND THEY FALL BACK.`
then, large: `SHALL I NOT DRINK IT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step forward in one hard moment. Settle, and breathe. Think of something hard that's coming toward you. A conversation you're dreading, a bill, a diagnosis, an apology you owe. Notice the urge to hide in the trees until it finds you. Now picture yourself stepping forward first, calm, and saying, in your own way, here I am. Breathe there. If you pray, you can ask for that kind of courage. If you don't, simply rehearse the first step. The bell holds the time.
Malchus. The high priest's servant whose ear Peter cut off in the garden, the only name John gives among the soldiers.
Your line: I am he. Today, take the first step toward the hard thing you pictured, before it comes looking for you. Day six hundred forty-two.

643.title: By the charcoal fire (John 18:12–27)
643.hook: Peter warms himself and denies him
643.howItsDone: Peter's denial is read in churches during Holy Week, and in Christian art a rooster beside Peter recalls it, a reminder both of failure and of forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, torches in the garden, Malchus's ear cut off, and two words that knocked soldiers to the ground. Your line was I am he. Did you take the first step? Day six hundred forty-three.

Two scenes are happening at once tonight, and John cuts between them like a film editor. Inside, Jesus is being questioned by Annas, father-in-law of the high priest Caiaphas. Outside, in the courtyard, it's cold. Servants and officers have built a fire, and they're standing around it with their hands out. And there, among them, is Peter. Earlier tonight he said he would lay down his life for Jesus. Then he swung a sword in the garden. Now he's standing at a fire, trying to look like he belongs.

In the King James Bible: "And the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves: and Peter stood with them, and warmed himself." Three times, Peter is asked. First the girl who keeps the door: "Art not thou also one of this man's disciples? He saith, I am not." Then someone at the fire asks the same thing, and again he says, I am not. Then a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter cut off: "Did not I see thee in the garden with him?" And Peter denied again, "and immediately the cock crew." Now put this beside yesterday's scene. In the garden, Jesus said, ego eimi, I am. At the fire, Peter says, ouk eimi, I am not. John sets them almost side by side. One steps forward. One steps back into the crowd. And inside, at the very same time, Jesus is telling the high priest: I spoke openly to the world; ask the people who heard me. He's naming witnesses, and one of his own disciples is outside saying he isn't one. One more detail. The Greek word for this charcoal fire is anthrakia. John will use that same word for a fire once more, much later. Hold on to that; it comes back. Readers have long found Peter's denial painful and strangely hopeful at once. It's painful because it's so ordinary: he isn't tortured, just asked by a doorkeeper. And it's hopeful because the church remembers this same Peter as a leader, later on.
screen: `A FIRE OF COALS, FOR IT WAS COLD.`
`I AM, INSIDE; I AM NOT, OUTSIDE.`
then, large: `AND PETER STOOD WITH THEM, AND WARMED HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where you warm yourself. Settle, and breathe. Peter's fire was a comfort and a hiding place at the same time. Think about yours. The group you go along with. The joke you laugh at so you'll fit in. The silence you keep when someone you love isn't there to defend themselves. Don't scold yourself. Just notice, gently, where you stand to stay warm. If you pray, you can bring that place to God honestly. If you don't, simply name it to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Anthrakia. The Greek word for the charcoal fire where Peter warmed himself and said, three times, I am not.
Your line: warming himself. Today, when you catch yourself going along to stay comfortable, take one small step out of the crowd. Day six hundred forty-three.

644.title: What is truth? (John 18:28–38)
644.hook: Pilate asks and doesn't wait for an answer
644.carry: I find in him no fault at all
644.howItsDone: Christians read Jesus's trial before Pilate during Holy Week, and churches that say the Apostles' Creed name him in it: suffered under Pontius Pilate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter at the anthrakia, the charcoal fire, saying I am not. Your line was warming himself. Where did you step out of the crowd? Day six hundred forty-four.

Out, in, out again. In today's scene Pilate can't stay in one place. The priests who bring Jesus won't go into the governor's hall, John says, so they can keep themselves ready to eat the Passover. So Pilate goes out to them, then back in to the prisoner, then out again. Watch his feet as the morning goes on. And in the middle of all that coming and going, he asks a question as large as any in the Gospel, then heads for the door.

It's early morning. Jesus is brought to the Roman governor's headquarters. Pilate is the man who will soon say he has power to crucify, and the conversation shuttles back and forth between him and the prisoner. Pilate asks: are you a king? And Jesus answers, in the King James Bible, "My kingdom is not of this world." Then he says what he came for: "To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth. Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice." And Pilate says three words: "What is truth?" And then, John tells us, he went out again. He asks the biggest question in the room and walks away before anyone can answer. Four hundred years ago the English writer Francis Bacon opened an essay with this scene: "What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer." Was he jesting? Nobody knows his tone. Readers have heard it as sneering, as weary, as a politician who's heard too many sincere men. The Greek word for truth is aletheia, and in John it's more than correct information. Jesus has already said, I am the way, the truth, and the life. So in John's telling, Pilate asks what truth is while Truth is standing in front of him. The irony is the point. Then Pilate goes out and tells them, I find in him no fault at all. Let's look back. This week: courage in trouble, the hour, keep them, be one, the garden, the fire, and now a question left hanging.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.`
`BORN TO BEAR WITNESS TO THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait for an answer today. Settle, and breathe. Think of a question you've been asking without really waiting for the answer. How are you doing, said in passing. What do you think, said while already reaching for your phone. Maybe a question you ask God, or yourself, and then change the subject. Pick one. For these minutes, ask it again, slowly, and then don't move on. Just wait. If you pray, you can ask it in prayer and leave a silence afterward. The bell holds the time.

original.note: Greek: what is truth? aletheia, truth; in John, more than correct facts: something you can be 'of'.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pilate asks a philosophy question.
what it means: the man with the power in the room asks what truth is, and walks out before the answer.
what a scholar hears: the irony John sets up ('I am the truth', 14:6), and Pilate's restless shuttling, out to the accusers and in to the prisoner (18:29–38), staging the question.
